code: sub <- df[df$Dataset == "IllusionGameValidation", ] rt <- sub$RT  nll <- function(p, gf, free_w = TRUE) {   mu <- p[1]; sg <- exp(p[2]); nd <- exp(p[3])   w <- if (free_w) plogis(p[4]) else 0   d <- ifelse(rt > nd, dlnorm(pmax(rt - nd, 1e-300), mu, sg), 0)   v <- -sum(log((1 - w) * d + w * gf(rt)))   if (is.finite(v)) v else 1e10 }  fitm <- function(gf, free_w = TRUE) {   st <- c(log(median(rt) - 0.2), log(0.5), log(0.2), qlogis(0.01))   if (!free_w) st <- st[1:3]   o <- optim(st, nll, gf = gf, free_w = free_w,              control = list(maxit = 8000, reltol = 1e-10))   c(exp(o$par[3]), if (free_w) plogis(o$par[4]) else 0, -o$value) }  sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(candidates), function(nm) {   r <- fitm(candidates[[nm]])   data.frame(component = nm, ndt = r[1], poutlier = r[2], logLik = r[3]) })) r0 <- fitm(candidates[[1]], free_w = FALSE) sens <- rbind(sens, data.frame(component = "none (poutlier = 0)",                                ndt = r0[1], poutlier = 0, logLik = r0[3])) rownames(sens) <- NULL  fitinfo <- list(n = nrow(sub), n_ppt = length(unique(sub$Participant)),                 min_rt = min(rt)) #> ndt across all seven components: 0.322 to 0.331 s (9 ms range)

title: Assessing Reliability and Interindividual Variability
text: validation study typical repeated-measures design: 30 participants perform 80 trials three conditions, record reaction times. Looking raw distributions, three conditions nearly indistinguishable, nothing suggests B C differ interesting way.
code: # The data are generated from a **shifted LogNormal** process (see cogmod's # cogmod_lognormal() family): a non-decision time `ndt` - the incompressible # encoding + motor delay - to which a LogNormal-distributed decision time is # added. # # Because we are simulating the data, we get to decide what is true, and we make # the two effects *deliberately* different: # # - **A vs. B**: a small but extremely **consistent** effect. Every participant #   is slowed down by about the same amount (the between-participant SD of the #   effect is tiny, 0.01). There is essentially no interindividual variability. # - **A vs. C**: an effect with a population mean of **exactly zero**, but a very #   large between-participant SD (0.30). Some participants are dramatically #   slowed down by condition C, others are dramatically speeded up.  set.seed(14)  n_participants <- 30 n_trials <- 80  # Per condition ndt <- 0.15  # Non-decision time (s): no response can occur before that  participants <- data.frame(   Participant = sprintf("S%02d", 1:n_participants),   # Overall speed: participants differ substantially from one another   Intercept = rnorm(n_participants, mean = log(0.6), sd = 0.20),   # A vs. B: small effect, (almost) identical for everybody   Effect_B = rnorm(n_participants, mean = 0.10, sd = 0.01),   # A vs. C: no effect on average, but huge interindividual variability   Effect_C = rnorm(n_participants, mean = 0.00, sd = 0.30) )  sim <- expand.grid(   Trial = 1:n_trials,   Condition = c("A", "B", "C"),   Participant = participants$Participant,   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) |>   left_join(participants, by = "Participant") |>   mutate(     # Trial-level mean of the *decision* time, on the log scale     meanlog = Intercept +       if_else(Condition == "B", Effect_B, 0) +       if_else(Condition == "C", Effect_C, 0),     # Generate RTs, adding within-participant (trial-to-trial) noise, and shift     # the whole distribution by the non-decision time     RT = ndt + rlnorm(n(), meanlog = meanlog, sdlog = 0.22),     Participant = factor(Participant),     Condition = factor(Condition)   ) |>   arrange(Participant, Condition, Trial) |>   select(Participant, Trial, Condition, RT) ggplot(sim, aes(x = RT, fill = Condition)) +   geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("A" = "grey40", "B" = "purple", "C" = "orange")) +   labs(     title = "Raw RT distributions by condition",     subtitle = "All trials pooled across participants: the three conditions look alike",     x = "Reaction Time (s)", y = "Density"   ) +   theme_minimal()

text: Beta-Binomial common default bounded count data, though wasn’t designed . distribution consists two-stage mixture: conditional success probability p, response follows Binomial(n,p)Binomial(n, p), p varies according Beta distribution. lets absorb extra-binomial variation (overdispersion) arising raters differ systematically response tendencies. model makes sense rating literally count successes (e.g. items endorsed checklist), single holistic judgment K-point scale, ’s better understood descriptive tool model response process . Note: Beta-Binomial distribution brms defined [0, n], need shift ratings 1 (1-6 -> 0-5). Discrete Beta model (Sciandra, 2024) developed modeling discrete rating data, .e., discrete responses fixed integer scale (1-K). assumes observed rating discretised counterpart continuous, unobservable latent response, rather estimating K−1K-1 threshold parameters (like Ordinal model), Discrete Beta fixes thresholds evenly spaced points, instead lets Beta distribution govern proportions. reverses usual logic (fixed distribution, estimated thresholds) , Beta distribution can take wide range shapes (including non-monotonic convex shapes like “J” “U” shapes many ordinal models struggle reproduce), yields distribution highly flexible remarkably parsimonious, requiring two parameters regardless many categories scale . Note: Beta-Discrete implementation cogmod allows “hurdle” (zero-inflated) component (pzero argument), pinned zero formula use pure Beta-Discrete distribution. Ordinal models (also known cumulative models) posit continuous latent variable, partitioned K−1K-1 estimated thresholds. thresholds freely estimated rather fixed, model doesn’t assume equally-spaced categories. maps onto signal-detection accounts ordinal judgment, continuous perception filtered response criteria can unevenly spaced (e.g. reluctance use extremes). flexibility comes cost extra parameters relative Beta-Discrete, thresholds parameters estimated arbitrary latent scale, really interpretable . Furthermore, threshold parameters highly sample-dependent, comparing latent estimates across different populations notoriously difficult, introduces challenges measurement invariance , ultimately, replicability. instance, fitting cumulative model new sample can yield different set threshold estimates, differences necessarily reflect changes underlying cognitive process, may instead arise shifts latent scale response criteria. Consequently, parameter estimates obtained independently fitted ordinal models often directly comparable, complicating cross-study replication meta-analytic synthesis unless common latent scale explicitly established. can compare models together using loo package. code: set.seed(33)  df <- data.frame() for(x in seq(0.2, 0.8, by = 0.1)) {   rating <- rcogmod_betadiscrete(n=500, mu = x, phi = 3, k = 6)   df <- rbind(df, data.frame(x = x, rating = rating)) }  df |>   ggplot(aes(x = rating)) +   geom_bar(stat = "count", fill = "#2196F3") +   labs(title = "Rating Distribution", x = "Score", y = "Density") +   theme_minimal() f <- bf(   rating | trials(5) ~ x,   phi ~ x,   family = brms::beta_binomial() )   m_betabinomial <- brm(f,   data = data_modify(df, rating = rating - 1),    family = brms::beta_binomial(), init = 0,   chains = 4, iter = 500, backend = "cmdstanr",  )  m_betabinomial <- brms::add_criterion(m_betabinomial, "loo")  # For later model comparison f <- bf(   rating | vint(6) ~ x,   phi ~ x,   pzero = 0,  # No zero-inflation   family = cogmod_betadiscrete() )  m_betadiscrete <- brm(f,   data = df, stanvars = cogmod_stanvars(f), init = 0,   chains = 4, iter = 500, backend = "cmdstanr" )  m_betadiscrete <- brms::add_criterion(m_betadiscrete, "loo")  # For later model comparison f <- bf(   rating ~ x,   disc ~ x,   family = brms::cumulative() )  m_cumulative <- brm(f,   data = df, family = brms::cumulative(), init = 0,   chains = 4, iter = 500, backend = "cmdstanr" )  m_cumulative <- brms::add_criterion(m_cumulative, "loo")  # For later model comparison loo::loo_compare(m_betabinomial, m_betadiscrete) |>   parameters::parameters() pred <- rbind(   estimate_prediction(m_betabinomial, ci = NULL,                        iterations = 100, keep_iterations = TRUE) |>     reshape_iterations() |>     data_modify(iter_value = iter_value + 1, Model = "Beta-Binomial"),   estimate_prediction(m_betadiscrete, ci = NULL,                        iterations = 100, keep_iterations = TRUE) |>     reshape_iterations() |>     data_modify(Model = "Beta-Discrete"),   estimate_prediction(m_cumulative, ci = NULL,                        iterations = 100, keep_iterations = TRUE) |>     reshape_iterations() |>     data_modify(Model = "Ordinal") )         pred_counts <- pred |>    dplyr::summarize(n = dplyr::n(), .by = c("Model", "iter_group", "iter_value")) |>    dplyr::summarize(n_median = median(n),             ci_low = quantile(n, 0.025),             ci_high = quantile(n, 0.975),             .by = c("Model", "iter_value"))   p <- df |>   ggplot(aes(x = rating)) +   geom_bar(stat = "count", fill = "#2196F3") +   geom_line(data = pred_counts, aes(x = iter_value, y = n_median), color = "#FF5722", linewidth = 1) +   geom_pointrange(     data = pred_counts,     aes(x = iter_value, y = n_median, ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high),     color = "#FF5722", size = 1   ) +   labs(title = "Rating Distribution", x = "Score", y = "Density") +   theme_minimal() +   facet_wrap(~Model) p

text: Writing \(\alpha = \mu \phi\) \(\beta = (1 - \mu)\phi\) shape parameters underlying Beta distribution, probability mass function (Sciandra et al., 2024, eq. 2) $$P(R = j) = F_B(j/k; \alpha, \beta) - F_B((j-1)/k; \alpha, \beta), \quad j = 1, \dots, k$$ \(F_B\) Beta CDF. rcogmod_betadiscrete() uses equivalent, faster generative representation: draw continuous \(X \sim Beta(\alpha, \beta)\) set \(R = \lceil k X \rceil\), clipped [1, k]. pzero > 0, hurdle added 0: probability pzero response 0, probability 1 - pzero generated Discrete Beta distribution described , .e. $$P(R = 0) = \code{pzero}, \quad P(R = j) = (1 - \code{pzero}) \times [F_B(j/k) - F_B((j-1)/k)], \quad j = 1, \dots, k$$ Special cases: mu = 0.5, phi = 1 (.e. alpha = beta = 1): reduces discrete Uniform distribution 1:k. alpha, beta < 1: "U"/"J"-shaped, mass concentrated tails. alpha, beta > 1: concave, mass concentrated around middle category. phi -> Inf (mu fixed): mass concentrates single category. pzero = 0: reduces pure Discrete Beta model (hurdle). Scale 0:N 0 hurdle (e.g., mix genuine/excess "zero" response ordinal 1:N scale): keep data -, use vint(N) (.e., total number categories minus hurdle category), let pzero estimated (optionally predictors, pzero ~ x).
